originalPipeline.explanation: Successful process exit did not constitute valid content. The two historical-source validation failures remain genuine failed original records; subsequent editorial recovery is recorded separately.

originalAndAuthorIssueResolutions.independentConclusion: Both original generator processes exited successfully but their source validations failed. Exact source URL binding now includes the retained English Wiktionnaire record and newly read Etymonline history. Their original failed validations remain retained, not relabelled as successful.
The pronunciation notes now teach a single syllable, the r before n in the American transcription, and the born/borne homophony. The obsolete-IPA production language and self-comparison are absent.
Born is identified as a participle and adjective rather than an infinitive; bear and bore have correct roles. The will be born example prevents an absolute past-only rule.
All six original birth-group examples and translations were read. They distinguish in for year/place, on for a specified day, at for clock time, into for family background and to for parents.

The birth-condition group is distinct from natural aptitude and has two separate examples. With can occur in either context without becoming a universal talent marker. The final revision adds a clear born blind collocation.
The note separates adjectival natural ability from nominal a natural at something. Learned/acquired are limited to ability or trait origins, not presented as direct replacements in a born leader.

Active childbearing has borne and formal passive agent borne by are supported by the independently read MLA and Oxford bear material. Ordinary be born remains the main birth-fact construction; by is not indiscriminately banned as a preposition.

The four figurative-origin examples, translations and notes correctly distinguish an idea coming into existence from causes expressed with of/out of/from. The explanation does not teach born from plus city as ordinary birthplace usage.

Old English boren is correctly treated as the participle of beran, with the relevant childbirth meaning explained. Carrying/endurance and the animal noun bear are distinguished. Conflicting spelling-split dates are not adopted; modern verb forms are not drawn as borrowing stages.

Bear is now shown as a verb, not the animal noun or caring. The final original bridge example clearly demonstrates the infinitive after cannot. Newborn adjective/noun and inborn quality meanings were independently confirmed on actual Oxford pages; aptitude does not eliminate practice.

All four extension examples were read: born and bred includes upbringing, not born yesterday concerns credulity, silver-spoon concerns privileged upbringing without claiming laziness, and place-born does not assert citizenship or upbringing.

There were no original model reviewer files or patches. This is an AI editorial recovery plus an independent AI full reading. No new model CLI, original patch replay, audio audition or human-teacher certification is claimed.

sourceEvidence.text: The editors distinguish passive reports of birth using born from active childbearing with borne. Borne also appears when a passive construction emphasizes the birth action and names the mother with by. Born can describe something resulting from an experience, including the preposition from. This does not turn every preposition after born into an interchangeable birth-place marker.

sourceEvidence.text: Born continues Old English boren, a past participle of beran. The linked bear material on the same page includes carrying and endurance as well as giving birth and producing. The relevant historical branch here is childbearing. The page also records later descriptions of qualities possessed from birth. Its different notes give inconsistent dating for the born/borne distinction, so no exact separation date is adopted.
